utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis along with Gerard Dobbyn, Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Igor Pantelic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could -- yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to inquire as the witness was coming in. I had sent an e-mail communication to Ms. Featherstone last night concerning the request for estimates about the remaining 92 bis witnesses we propose in relation to adjudicated facts, and I indicated in an e-mail we'd asked to have until Thursday to provided that information. I wanted to confirm that that was satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Before Mr. Krgovic resumes his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I resume, I have a few corrections for the transcript. Page 49, when the witness was reading the transcript, the line 21, there's a name appearing there. It should say Vojo Kupresanin came in person. That's one correction. Next, page 51, when I mentioned the name of Stojan Zupljanin, his name is Bajazid Jahic. It was not recorded properly. These were the corrections I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While on that topic, Mr. Sivac, did you know Mr. Bajazid Jahic, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin's deputy, he was a policeman from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall him being a soccer player of the team called Napret [phoen]. He was a policeman and he did not have a very nice character. He was quite short-tempered and we all ascribed that to his profession. I remember him before the war and the lasts time I saw him in Sanski Most, I think it was in 1996 or 1997 when he was with the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, yesterday we left it off discussing Hambarine and the incident of the 24th of May. It took place between Hambarine and Ljubija on a road; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a local road between Prijedor and Ljubija which takes you through Hambarine, a Muslim settlement called Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, you testified something I wanted to ask you about. Did you know about an incident at a check-point near Kozarac just prior to the attack on Kozarac? There seems to have been a Serb soldier killed there as well as a few of them wounded. It was actually on a check-point which leads through Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to take this with a grain of salt. No one ever submitted credible evidence of any patrols being attacked in Kozarac. It was simply a figment of imagination in order to mobilise Serb soldiers. That was used as an excuses to launch the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac. That incidents did not take place. It was invented, fabricated, in order to come up with an excuse for what was to happen the very same day after Hambarine were shelled. I can expand that. On 23rd and 24th, Hambarine was shelled. The same day, the 24th, around noon, the crazed commander, Stojan Zupljanin via Radio Prijedor, issued a threatening message to the people of Kozarac who had been encircled for a while, completely cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Commander Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Radmilo Zeljaja. He said that the people of Kozarac, unless they hand over -- handed over their weapons and accepted the new Croatian authorities, he would raze Kozarac to the ground and so it was. After that, instead of the sign-post Kozarac, his soldiers put up a new sign-post which said Radmilovo, after their commander Radmilo Zeljaja, who destroyed Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What unit was that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 304th or the 34th Motorised Brigade. It changed names and it was transformed as different elements of the Serb forces were attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I asked you about that incident in Hambarine. It is then when you heard some information to the effect that there had been an incident on the check-point in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was invented. It was a figment of imagination of some journalists. That information had originally arrived from the municipal information staff. As I said, it was invented. One needs to come up with an incidents in order to mobilise the army to have a reason to do so. No one ever published who was wounded or killed in that incident, whereas for the Hambarine incident, which indeed took place, we know the names of the participants on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Kozarac is along the main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the incident you mentioned happened along that road at a check-point; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that incident. I repeat, it was a virtual incident. It did not exist. It was an excuse for Radmilo Zeljaja to go about destroying Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, weren't these incidents part of the plan you referred to yesterday to have diversions in order to attack certain Serb units and facilities? Was it not part of that plan?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no plan, Mr. Krgovic. The group around Slavko Ecimovic, as I said, was a group of people who feared Serb retaliation, once the Serbs took over Prijedor. They simply gathered, organised themselves, spontaneously, although they had very few weapons. If one looks at the way they thought, because there were very few of them, well, you're wrong about this. I have to explain. Slavko had about 20 men. And at that part of the left bank of the Sana river, which included a string of Muslim villages, there were some other groups. They were not united. Only after Izmet Mesic-Hadzija, who was an international criminal who spent most of his life in various European prisons and he was a drug addict, only after he had managed to persuade Slavko because that is what he was instruct to do in the barracks to gather all those groups, Slavko did so trying to take over or liberate Prijedor. It was only after that that they became united. They had never been together before that. When discussing this with those who survived, I asked them what were your thoughts at the outset? And they said, We just wanted to stay low, to save our lives. Even before the Serbs took over, their property became target to explosive devices, and people issued threats. After they gathered, they thought along these lines: Bihac and the Bihac area which was under B and H control was 100 kilometres away. We thought we should try to break through to join the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At first, we also thought that because of what had happened in Prijedor and Kozarac, we should try at least by initiating small diversionary actions to do something. However since we were short of explosives and weapons, we gave it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this Hadzija, is it the same Hadzija whom you mentioned in your book when you said that he was a fighter, you said he was brave and managed to disarm a Serb officer and organise the attack? Is that the same Hadzija?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we write books, we sort of try to add things in literary terms to make things a bit prettier. The book was written in 1993 and 1994 when did I not have all the relevant documents which shed further light about the role of Izmet Mesic-Hadzija. That book far precedes my receiving any relevant documents about his role in the whole thing. I should say this as well, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, please explain to us once again where we are going with all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wanted to ask the witness, although he expanded his answers, about the witness [as interpreted]. I wanted to know whether it was the same person whom he mentioned yesterday. However, the witness went off on a tangent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please answer my questions only. Your reach is quite encompassing but it does not clarify things sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you were shown a photograph yesterday by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P01531 shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You identified this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in so that we could see the person behind him, so that we could see the people standing just behind the fence, to the right of this man. The person in blue shorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, can you see that person?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite a poor photograph. But can I make him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And doesn't he look quite normal? He even seems to have some fat?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it very much depends who he is. I don't know whether he arrived in Keraterm from Trnopolje and Omarska or whether he arrived directly. People in Keraterm had more privilege, so to speak, position. They enjoyed the presence of their wives and children there. And they were allowed to cook for themselves. However, those arriving from Keraterm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to see whether you can identify this person.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the far right side of the photograph and zoom in, please. Further to the right. All the way to the end. Further to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The person question see behind the journalist.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He is wearing black pants. Can you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. The face is quite dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you see the neck -- the person standing next to him in red shorts?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that these people look quite well fed, even above the average?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were probably well fed in Omarska and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the only thin person in the photograph is the person, Penny Marshall is talking to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Mr. Krgovic. You are taking things out of context. This is just a small detail. Admir Djulkic [phoen] is shown here but he is only one of the people who survived it all. For the most part, people resembled him. However, it all depended on one's build and one's metabolism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that Mr. Djulkic had been thin before the war?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He used to be an athlete. He was goal keeper in a soccer team. He was well-built.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you will agree that Mr. Djulkic, as compared to what he used to look like, he did not change much?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not. Actually his last name is Djulkic, Ahmed. He used to be well-built. He was quite normal in that sense. However, you can see this for yourself. This is what happened to him after his time in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We were in the same room with Burho and Mujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, I have just a few question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Sivac. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. O'Sullivan asked you some questions about crimes committed by local paramilitary members who returned to Prijedor from Croatia. And specifically you were asked when the war broke out in Bosnia, these same paramilitaries, and he was referring to ones formed by Milan Andzic, were the ones committing crimes and looting to a large extent in Prijedor, weren't they? And you agreed they were. And for reference, this is transcript page 13208, line 21. Now just to be clear, Mr. Sivac, what time-period were you talking about here? Was this before or after the April 30 takeover on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you are referring to the unit that was funded by Milan Andzic and headed by Momir Radanovic, Cigo, that unit was also infamous for the crimes that they had committed in Western Slavonia and also for looting. And from Western Slavonia, they would bring in transport, war booty, as they referred to it. When the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor municipality began on the 30th of May, when they began by destroying Kozarac and Prijedor, they were especially infamous in the crimes that they comitted in Kozarac. And to explain this to a Trial Chamber, let me just say that 95 per cent of the population of Kozarac was Muslim, and a large number of people from Kozarac had worked in Europe or were working in Europe as guest workers and they had earned a lot of money there which they brought back and built homes in Kozarac, and so on. So this was a challenge of sorts for these Chetniks to actually try and take control of Kozarac. So in May, Kozarac was looted and it was completely looted and the booty or the loot, actually, was transported to Omarska and Milan Andzic was the person who had control over this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to look now to another question you were asked by Mr. O'Sullivan. He asked you about your prior testimony in Brdjanin, and in -- in particular, where you had said that after the April 30 takeover paramilitary formations and gangs became active in Prijedor municipality and they took justice into their own hands, and you agreed that you had said that in Brdjanin. Now, my question to you is: Are you aware of the police, after April 30, taking any steps to stop those crimes? Are you aware of police arresting any paramilitary members or gang members for crimes committed against non-Serbs after April 30 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. And even the complaints -- the complaints that were submitted by citizens of Serb nationality against these paramilitary units and the criminals who had come from Serbia or from the Knin Krajina, to the effect that they are terrorising people in Prijedor and robbing them, the police of Prijedor responded by issuing a statement that it was not capable to stop that because those paramilitary units were, as it were, under the control or under the protection of the military authorities because they used them to do their dirty work for them in certain military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, are you aware of an incident where four Muslims were killed in a place called Jelovac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see how this line of question was related to my cross-examination or the cross-examination ducted by Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Although we didn't have the benefit of translation, I anticipated that objection, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn, how does this arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my interpretation, and perhaps I'm incorrect, that the thrust of the questioning from Mr. O'Sullivan was that crimes being committed in Prijedor around this time were solely being committed by paramilitaries, that there was no police involvement. So I'm hoping to explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No microphone, apparently. Oh yes. Your Honour, my question to Mr. Sivac was quite specific and Mr. Dobbyn has referred to it, and that was his testimony in Brdjanin and that was his understanding of the events at the time, and he's given that answer, and to move into any specifics does not at all arise from what Mr. Sivac knew from his personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] sorry, I don't have a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I have it now. Sorry. Your Honour, he was asked -- the question was put to him in a specific way, that paramilitary formations and gangs became active in Prijedor municipality and took justice into their own hands. He agreed with that proposition. Now I am hoping to expand on that and see whether he was saying it was exclusively those groups or whether police were also doing things at the time. The wording of the question as it was put to him, he agreed to that proposition that there were paramilitaries and gangs involved in crimes, but he wasn't perhaps given the opportunity to -- to see if there was any other groups beyond that involved. It was a response to a very specific question and I want to see what the extend of his knowledge was, as to which groups were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed. But a narrowly focussed question, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, I understand that this incident in Jelovac, you say, that was part of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour, and that's what I hope to clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So I will ask the question again, Mr. Sivac. Were you aware of an incidents, the killing of four Muslims in Jelovac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was well aware of it. Jelovac is on the main road from Prijedor to Bosanska Dubica, and a group of four Muslims from Brezicani, among whom Jusuf Kuckovic, headed on a tractor to collect hay for some farmers in Jelovac, that's a village, when they were stopped by a group of armed Serbs who killed the four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't. This proceeded all these other events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you able to give a rough indication? Was it 1992, was it another year?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was some time in early 1992 or in late 1991, but I can't really say with precision or with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the individuals responsible for these killings?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we object. There's absolutely no foundation to go beyond these preliminary questions which have shown that Mr. Sivac is unsure of the event, when it happened, he -- he heard about it. He certainly -- it's not within his personal knowledge to speak in any detail about this. He just told us that he doesn't know anything other than what he heard from unnamed sources. In our submission, this is not appropriate for any further exploration on the details of what may have transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, in any event, Mr. Dobbyn, how would the names be relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, the names may be relevant, Your Honour, if he also knows which organs, if any, these individuals were members of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, I think have you taken this as far as you could, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, were you familiar with the Prijedor Police Intervention Platoon?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we learned about the intervention platoon as soon as the Serb takeover took place. This was a group of heartless people, among whom there was a number of Prijedor criminals who were under the direct control of Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And are you aware if this group was involved in any attacks on non-Serbs in Prijedor, or any other crimes?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they actually did the dirtiest jobs for the Prijedor police and they participated in almost all of the actions conducted by the police or the army, in co-ordination between the two, in the area of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on to something slightly different. And this was questions put to you again yesterday from Mr. O'Sullivan about the attack on Kozarac, and it was put to you that Andzic's paramilitaries participated in the attack on Kozarac, and you agreed that they had, together with the 5th Kozarac Brigade? Do you recall that exchange yesterday? And this is at transcript page 13209.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I just want to clarify this, if possible. In your Stakic testimony, which as part of your 92 ter package, at transcript page 6764, you said that during the Serb takeover of Kozarac, the Serb military and police killed the majority of the police employees of the Kozarac police station. So just to be clear, Mr. Sivac, were the police also involved in this attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, of course. The Serb police, from Prijedor, at the head of which was Simo Drljaca, and in co-ordination with the army, they took part in the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And these police employees that were killed, did you personally see any of the corpses of these killed policemen?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group of police officers from Kozarac who surrendered to the Serb army immediately following the shelling of Kozarac, together with their commander, Osmo Didovic, as far as I know, was shot dead right there on the spot close to the place where they surrendered to the Serb forces. After my first -- after the first time I was taken to Omarska, in a police vehicle, Brane Bolta and another active-duty policeman who escorted us to the Omarska, they stopped the van, the police van, on the spot where this had taken place, and I got out of the van, together with them to take a look, and in a small river, or stream, rather, near a bridge, we could see a number of bodies in blue uniforms. Tomo Stojakovic turned and looked at me and when he saw that I was looking at those bodies, he said, Well, Simo, all these men are former colleagues from Kozarac. To the right of the police van, which had stopped in a ditch, I saw another body, which was face down, and there was a cloud of flies above him and then we found a sheet of nylon nearby so we covered the body, and when we got back to the police van, Tomo Stojakovic used a radio to inform the duty service of the SUP in Prijedor to get in touch with the services, the municipal services, who were in charge of sanitation to come to that spot and collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, the last thing I'd like to ask you about, Mr. Sivac, is some questions -- line of questioning from Mr. Krgovic yesterday regarding the attack on Prijedor. And in the course of that line of questioning, Mr. Krgovic stated that the defense position was that the attack or counter-attack on Prijedor was a military operation carried out by a local brigade commander who had nothing to do with Stojan Zupljanin. This is at transcript page 13256, line 23. And I'd just like to ask you one question about that. In your Stakic testimony, talking about the events in Prijedor on 30th of May, you stated: "At the beginning, it was just light infantry weapons, Slavko's people, people from Slavko's group had such weapons. Later on, the unequal confrontation between Slavko's group and the Prijedor SUP members and the Serb army led by Zoran Karlice and Radmilo Zeljaja, Slavko Ecimovic's people did not stand a chance." That was at transcript page 6574. And I just would like to ask you, Mr. Sivac, do you stand by that testimony that the Prijedor police were also involved in the fighting in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And their involvement was very active. They had two armoured APCs, and all the active-duty and reserve police officers were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And that's all the questions I have for you, Mr. Sivac. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I would like you to look at a document that is on the Prosecutor's list of documents under tab 10. It's 65 ter list 02238. Do you recognise this man seen from the back?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. This is somebody else. This is not Ahmet Olic [phoen]. I can't identify the man because his back is turned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have back on the screen the 65 ter number 02240, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a full picture, as we say, and the previous photo was from the back, a shot taken from the back. I do see that this man is wearing black trousers and a red -- red pants underneath, and his position, the way he stands, is the same, except that here the photo was taken from the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But you -- you can't say it's the same man.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just judging by the clothes, the black pants and the red underpants, I would assume that it is the same man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And in -- in that case, that it is the same man -- could we have 02238 back on the screen, please. So if this would be the same man, could you then comment on the size of his trousers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can see that his pants are large, too large that they're sort of falling off, and he had lost so many kilos, that even his pants, or trousers won't keep about his waist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if this is the gentlemen that you say was your friend that we saw from the face in the other photo, it's not his normal way of wearing trousers that are that -- that large -- that are much too large for him. It's not that way. You know him before he got into the camps?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have known him for a very long time. We grew up together. We lived on the same street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But my question is, this is the not the way he used to wear his trousers?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He wore normal trousers like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, could I just put one additional question to you to clarify the answer that you gave to the Prosecutor during his re-direct examination. Because you told the Court that, in relation to the crimes allegedly perpetrated by the paramilitary units in Prijedor, the police in Prijedor did not take any steps to prevent this from happening or to arrest any members of the paramilitary groups for the reason that they were under the command of the army, so the police had no authority over them. Is that a correct re-statement of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. They served -- they worked for both the police and the army. Both the police and army used them when they needed someone to do their dirty work for them. So the ones and the others, they both protected them. The statement that was broadcast on Radio Prijedor and was published in the "Kozarski Vjesnik" was to the effect that, allegedly, they could not take any steps against these people because in future operations they would be charged with carrying out certain tasks, or assignments, for the benefit of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, and thank you for this clarification. But tell us, Mr. Sivac, how -- how would these paramilitary units come under the authority of the police? Do you know that? Did the police chief in Prijedor actually issue orders or requests for assistance from these paramilitary groups? I'm -- Mr. Sivac, I'm interested in getting a better picture of the -- of the patterns of control that applied during these times in Prijedor, if you can help us with that. Because you had the army and the soldiers and then you had the police forces, and they would not necessarily be any Joint Command over these people. I would assume that the police chief would be in charge of his policemen; and the army, responsible army officer, would be responsible and in charge and in control of the armed forces. So under which conditions or circumstances would, say, a soldier or a member of the paramilitary groups come under the authority of the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this. At that time, a great deal of convicts were released from the correctional facilities where they served their sentences. Basically they all joined either the police or the army to do, as I've already mentioned, the dirtiest jobs of all. These were natural-born criminals. Let's take the example of Zoran Zigic. He was murder. He had killed a man before the war. After having served his sentence, he joined quite normally the paramilitary units in Prijedor after everything began happening. Nobody knows was unit he belonged to. He kept changing his uniforms, but he was the most ruthless person of all. He would come in to camps with his group, killing and mistreating detainees, and he also mistreated Serb civilians in Prijedor. He was completely out of control. But he could be used for some things, say, during combat, or during mop-up operations where he always went in first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when Mr. Zigic and his group operated, would that be at the requests of either the chief of police or the local army commander? Did Mr. Zigic operate according to any schedule or orders or plans that had been established by the authorities in the area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a maverick basically working on his own and if he didn't like someone, he just killed them. But he also did tasks for the security service. However, Djordje Dosen, aka Djole, is somebody who was not prosecuted because he had died in the meantime. He was Zigic's counterpart. He was always with Dusan Jankovic wearing a police uniform and is guilty of countless murders following the orders of either the police or someone else, some other sources of his. Unfortunately, he passed away a few years back and was never prosecuted. He was always sitting in a police car together with Dusan Jankovic at the time. They would go up and down through Prijedor and Djole Dosen was the executioner following orders which most probably came from the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question: The situation that you have described for us relating to Prijedor and the Prijedor area, I understand would also cover the Kozarac municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, Kozarac, administratively speaking, was a local commune not a municipality. Save for the town of Prijedor, the municipality included a number of local communes, some 30 of them. The largest of those were Kozarac, Ljubija and Omarska, in terms of the number of residents. There was a number of other smaller ones, such as the Muslim settlements on the left bank of the Sana river and Serb settlements on the right bank of the river, just below Mount Kozara. There are a number of Serb settlements there which were also small local communes. Only the local communes of Kozarac and Ljubija, as well as Omarska, had their respective police station. The rest was covered by the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We better be absolutely sure that we get this right. So I would wish to ask you yet another question just to clarify what you have just said. Namely, your assertion that the police took no steps in Prijedor to prevent crimes from being committed by the paramilitary units, did that statement also cover the Kozarac area, after the crimes were committed, as you have described it, in Kozarac? In other words, did the police take any steps to address the criminal events in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which specific crimes in Kozarac you have in mind. I don't remember having mentioned crimes and incidents in Kozarac. The crimes in Kozarac only took place after the takeover, after the 30th of May, when the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac took place. It -- actually in Kozarac it all began on the 24th of May, 1992. After heavy shelling, military -- paramilitary and police forces began ethnically cleansing Kozarac. The crimes which took place in Kozarac at that time is something that no one was ever called to account for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question, if I may, which follows Judge Harhoff's -- from Judge Harhoff's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, did you know that this Dosen and Zigic you mentioned were arrested by the military authorities and prosecuted before a military court for crimes committed over Muslims, as members of the RS army?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Zoran Zigic. He committed several murders of Serbs after the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac and Prijedor. He could not be reined in, and the Serb authorities simply handed him over to get rid of the idiot and the murder. As for Djole Dosen, he was never called to task. I don't know where you get that information from. He lived a free man and passed away due to natural causes after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether both Dosen and Zigic were prosecuted by a military court for crimes over non-Serbs? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, we thank you for your testimony before the Tribunal. Indeed, your continued assistance to the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, before the witness is formally released, your live application for the admission of your -- of the 92 package is now admitted and -- and marked accordingly. Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We have -- we take objection to five of the proffered exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we hear you, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So there are five exhibits we object to. Four of them are newspaper articles. The first one is 65 ter 2514. Well, I don't believe the tabs -- the tab -- the spreadsheet doesn't have a number. But it's the 13th -- if that helps, it's the 13th document. It's a -- it's an article from "Kozarski Vjesnik." It was read out loud by this witness during his testimony in the Stakic trial. Because, at that time no B/C/S translation existed. So it's part of the Stakic transcripts, but it is merely read into the record by the witness. He was asked no questions about it in Stakic and he was asked no questions about it here. On that basis, we say it has no probative value. It's just a newspaper article, freestanding. The other -- the four more examples are newspaper articles as well: 65 ter 10451; 65 ter 10452; and 65 ter 10453. Again, read into the record in the Stakic proceedings by the witness because there was no B/C/S, no questions asked of him then or here. Therefore, we object. It's our standing objection to newspaper articles. And the fifth document we take objection to is 65 ter 2414, which, in the Stakic trial at pages 6755, 6756, and that transcript is also being offered, on those pages, this witness told the Presiding Judge Schomburg that these documents were likely either forged or had been tampered with. Therefore, again, we say from this witness's own mouth he has described this document, 65 ter 2414, as being and I quote tampered, forged, and, therefore, we say it is an unreliable document and shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I hear Mr. Dobbyn, do you have anything on this application, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I support what Mr. O'Sullivan has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a couple of points to make with regards to this objection. The first is that the Trial Chamber issued a decision on Mr. Sivac's 92 ter package on the 2nd of October, 2009, and in that, it was found that these documents were integral parts of his testimony and on that basis, presuming that the package gets admitted as a whole, they would make part of that package. Now the Defence could have objected to that decision. There's been -- there was no appeal of that decision. Secondly, that as a general point, we would say that if there is going to be an objection taken to documents within a 92 ter package that that objection should be made at the start of the witness's testimony or even before the witness comes into court so that we then have an opportunity to address any issues that may arise with those documents with the witness while he is on the stand. And by this objection being made at the end, we haven't had a chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Dobbyn, isn't the reason why the practice that has been followed of waiting until the conclusion of cross-examination to act on the application to admit the package is precisely to allow any objections to be made by the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objections that are being made don't arise out of his testimony. We're given a limited time with 92 ter witnesses to put documents in through those witnesses, and so we have to rely, to a large extent, on what decisions we get from the Trial Chamber as to what documents can make up his 92 ter package. Now if we know ahead of time that certain objections taken to certain documents, we could then address that with the witness while he is on the stand. We can't go through every documents to hopefully foresee any issues that may come up and address them with the witness. We simply don't have the time or the opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I take your point in terms of the last-mentioned document. But in terms of the newspaper articles, isn't Mr. O'Sullivan's recollection correct, that -- as the approach that we have taken to newspaper articles and harking back to the October 2009 decision, the -- wouldn't the decision of the Trial Chamber have been that the 92 package, includes the -- for want of a better expression, trailing documents provided they're relevant; in other words, admissible. Isn't that what we would have said?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can say is reading from the finding -- the ruling in that decision it states that when admitting into evidence the prior statements and written statements of a witness pursuant to Rule 92 ter, we also admit all the accompanying documents, save those that were specifically identified in the motion for the reason that it views this evidence as an integral whole. So, Your Honours, our submission is that these documents were apparently reviewed when this decision was made and they were found to be integral to the 92 ter testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The order of the Trial Chamber is that the 92 package is admitted, save for the articles, the newspaper articles are not included. And in terms of the committee decision, it will be marked for identification, be separately marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I then may raise an issue and a question for future witnesses. In this case that was a decision made by the Trial Chamber where it appeared that it had considered those particular articles as being an essential part of his testimony and they were admitted. We relied on that. Now we have an objection after this witness has testified when we haven't had a chance to address any of these issues, and that evidence is gone. We need know in the future if that is still going to be the course. Because if we have a 92 package that is proposed and includes certain documents, if the Trial Chamber makes an initial finding that they are integral to the witness's prior testimony or his statement and we have limited time, an hour or two hours, or whatever it is for the witness, we, in most cases, are not going to address those documents because we don't have the time. If the Defence has an objection, I suggest it would be a more efficient course if they raise that specific evidence, that specific objection before the witness comes on and then we can deal with it. We may even agree that the objection is well taken and withdraw such an exhibit. But this is -- this is a bit of an ambush, we don't think it's a fair way to proceed, and we just want to know what the position is so we can deal with it most efficiently in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank counsel. We're going to return to this issue later because we have to give it some more consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- and returning to the witness, we -- you are now released and we wish you a safe journey back to your home, and we note that your testimony in this and previous trials has not been merely as an observer to events, but that you, yourself, having been the victim of some of these horrific incident, the Chamber expresses its sympathy to you. Thank you, sir. We wish you a safe journey back to your home. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and good bye.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to be given the opportunity to respond to what Mr. Hannis said to you, either now or if you want to deal with the issue later at your pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would hear you now because no doubt we are going to be discussing this among ourselves during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The point was this, Your Honour. The four newspaper articles we objected to were simply read into the record by the witness in Stakic, because there was no B/C/S translation. Prosecution was aware of that, as we were from reading the transcript. Under Rule 92 ter, the party calling the witness has the opportunity to ask further questions about the previous testimony. It's precisely on that point that the Prosecution is required, if they want to tender or have the witness expand upon the newspaper article, they do it during examination-in-chief. They did not do that. They should have been aware of that. Now, if the Prosecution had done that, there would have been no objection on our part. It is for the party to foresee this. We couldn't make an objection before the testimony because we didn't know if the Prosecution would address the newspaper articles with the witness. They didn't, and therefore we objected, just as we objected to the forged document. So the Prosecution knows what is in the previous testimony as we do. The Prosecution had the opportunity to question the witness on -- that previous testimony, including these newspaper articles, and they didn't. That's why we objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may reply. Your Honours, speaking specifically to those four newspaper articles, I -- I have less of a concern than I do about the general procedure. I agree. I have read some prior transcripts where I see that happen in some cases that documents were read in by a Prosecutor, doesn't appear any specific question was asked of a witness, and they were admitted, to my surprise. But my position is the most efficient process would be if the Defence has an objection to indicate that at the time that the 92 ter package is proposed. But when the Trial Chamber looks at it and make as decision and says it is an integral part of the testimony, then we feel, given the fact that we are limited to how much time we have with a 92 ter witness, that we can rely on that. If Mr. O'Sullivan had raised that before the witness came on and said, Okay, well either since have an objection to it, I'm going to have to deal with it and decide if I have to omit something else I want to during my limited one hour or two hours with a 92 ter witness. If he doesn't say anything then I am assuming he doesn't object to that, that has been admitted as part of the 92 ter package. That's all I'm asking. With regard to the newspaper articles, because of our general position about newspaper articles, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to intervene on that point, Mr. Hannis, and indicate that the -- as I said, we're going to have to return to this later. But the newspaper articles have -- how we approach those have bedevilled us from the time I have been participating in this exercise. So we can set that aside. And the -- probably the position that we have taken, I hope consistently, in terms of newspaper articles is something which counsel should be appreciated should be read alongside or integrated into how the 92 ter package is accepted, but in terms of the fifth item, the subject of being of persuaded other was I am inclined to agree with the position that you have made and now repeated that having been alerted, the Defence should have indicated to you their objection to -- to the committee report. As I said, we'll return to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry. Just one more matter with regards to the 92 ter package, unrelated to what we are talking about now, it's just while I remember. When it is admitted, we have -- his 92 ter package contains both official and unofficially transcripts of his prior testimony. The reason for that was that the past practice has been uncorrected -- unofficial transcripts have been going and as far as the 92 ter packages, and we have been highlighting those transcripts with the relevant portions. Now just recently, we understand from Registry that there's a problem with that, and they prefer that the official transcripts come in. So this 92 ter package includes both the official and the unofficial transcripts, the reason being that we need the marking, the highlighted portions to remain in there so that's why we are keeping the unofficial transcripts, and the unofficial need to be admitted under seal as apparently they have not yet been -- they were not checked for possible protected witnesses. So we would ask that those particular transcripts be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, we are not -- we haven't forgotten that -- this continuing problem, which is another -- which is a related issue but a separate issue. Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honours, I'm a bit confused now. It was our understanding that only the official transcripts are the ones which are admitted because the unofficial transcripts are unofficial and therefore there is -- there is a newer version of that same transcript afterwards, which is the official version of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you, Mr. Zecevic. You needn't be embarrassed about being confused, because you will recall that on at least two occasions before the break, we addressed this, and this is a matter that is still to be resolved. So everything that you say with respect makes perfect sense. We agree with the problem, how this is worked out on the ground at the Registry level, and at some point it is going to have to be resolved, but it is still being worked through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We may as well take the break now, although it is about two minutes early. So we would resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We apologise to counsel and the support staff for taking the Bench 30 minutes beyond the break when we should have resumed, but the ruling that we indicated that we may have been giving, we're not in a position to deal with this afternoon. It's a matter that is more complicated that appeared at first blush. The -- because of the 30-minute delay, we're thinking of the convenience of counsel, the support staff and the accused who were in court waiting and we are going to figure out how we are going to juggle the remainder of today's timing. Is the Prosecution ready with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honours. And maybe somewhat relate to what Your Honour just mentioned. If I may make an application. We request an hour and a half with this witness. The reason being she is a viva voce witness and we have a number of documents that the Trial Chamber hasn't had a chance to see yet that we'll tender through her. I note that we had to -- we chose to drop two Prosecutor witnesses that relate to this witness and, therefore, she is kind of making up the difference. It is possible that I will be very close to the hour that we originally estimated, but I just wanted, in the abundance of caution, to make a request at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we have noted your application, but we'll see where we stand at the end of the hour that you indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours. Because, like I said, perhaps I will be able to keep it within that time-frame. Because of the number of documents, I just wanted to give it a little bit of margin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I trust that can you hear me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, could I, first of all, then ask you to give us the solemn declaration and to read it out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. You may sit down. First of all, madam, welcome to the Tribunal, and thank you for coming to give your evidence. May I start by asking you to give us your full name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Biljana Simeunovic. I was born on 6th of November, 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I may ask you of your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Serbian. Madam, what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until June, I was a legal -- a senior legal counsel. And as of June, I was an investigating judge in the lower court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam, have you previously testified before this Tribunal or before any of the domestic courts in your country, in relations to matters relating to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well then. I will therefore just briefly explain to you how the proceedings unfold in these trials. You are being called as a witness by the Prosecution who is sitting to your right, and I suppose that you have already had the chance to meet with the Prosecutor, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Olmsted has requested one hour to conduct your examination-in-chief, and he has also indicated that he run a little over that time. But, in principle, your examination-in-chief should be completed by one hour, one hour and a half at the most. After that, the Defence counsels for Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin, who you see to your left, will be given the opportunity to cross-examine you, and the Defence counsel for Mr. Stanisic has asked for two hours in cross-examination; and counsel for Mr. Zupljanin has asked for one hour. This will certainly bring us into the proceedings for tomorrow also. Because we have to adjourn at 7.00. That's as far as we can go today, and then we will resume tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom also. Now, we have to have a break every 90 minutes because the tapes need to be turned, and so after approximately 90 minutes, we'll have a short break of approximately 20 minutes' time. If at any point, madam, you need to have a break or you feel a need to adjourn for a short while, then please let us know and we will comply with your request. After the cross-examination of the Defence counsels, the Prosecution, again, will have the opportunity to have a re-direct examination, and either after that, or at any point during your testimony, the Judges might put additional questions to you. So that's how the proceedings are going to unfold. Do you have any questions at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case, I only need to remind you that you are obliged to tell us the truth and the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and I should also remind you that there's a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete information to the Court here. With these words, madam, I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I first want to go very briefly over your legal background. You began working for the Bijeljina Basic Court in 1988; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned with regard to Judge Harhoff's questions but you were appointed as one of the judges of the Bijeljina Basic Court in 1992. Could you please give us, if you recall, the date of your formal appointment?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of June, 1992, I was appointed judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And do you recall who signed your appointment?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long did you remain as a basic court judge in Bijeljina, to what year?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but some time -- until some time in mid-1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from 1996 until 2001, you were a private attorney practising in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from 2003 to present, you have been a prosecutor, for the BiH State Court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: A prosecutor at the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. I want to return to June 1992. How many other basic court judges were appointed along with you for Bijeljina in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, 19 judges, including me, were appointed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Also in June, were a prosecutor and deputy prosecutors also appointed?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall how many?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: With a time that has elapsed, I think there were four prosecutors at the lower prosecutor's office, and I can't really say for certain how many there were in the higher prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned the higher prosecutor's office. Was there also a higher court in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us where were the offices of the basic court, the basic prosecutor, the higher court, and the higher prosecutor located? Were they in the same premises, or were they located separately?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: All of these were in the same premises, and that is still the case, and that was the case before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, as a basic court judge, did you participate in the criminal investigation of Vojin Vuckovic and members of his unit in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you later learn the name of Vuckovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, through documents, there were -- there was mention of Zuco, a nickname, and sometimes Yellow Wasps, but only after the war did I learn that they called themselves officially Yellow Wasps, but when I -- the court files that I had available, they had a different name that they used for their unit, one of their co-fighters who had been killed. I can't really recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to show you a few documents from that case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen 65 ter 2487.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a request to the investigating judge of the Lower Court Bijeljina dated 24 August, 1992. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: This was a request to conduct an investigation. It was submitted by the lower public prosecutor's office in Bijeljina against a number of individuals. And as can you see from the request, the charges were for the crime of aggravated theft, Article 148, paragraph 3, of the SRBH Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was assigned as investigative judge to this case?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was the investigating judge in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, the prosecutor writes that she is submitting along with this request the criminal report with annexes. Were you provided with those documents?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What would have been included in the annexes that she references?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the standard procedure. There would be a criminal report submitted by the police. At the time we used to refer to them as the organs of the interior. This criminal report then, together with annexes, would be submitted to the prosecutor's office, and then the prosecutor's office, based on the criminal report and the annexes, would submit a request for an investigation to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But with regard to the annexes, would that include any evidence that the police had collected up to that point, with regard to the crimes at issue?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The criminal report would list the annexes, and I think that perhaps in this request you would -- you could find that too, that the criminal report is submitted, together with the annexes, and the criminal report would list the annexes that are submitted, together with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. We'll look at the criminal report in a second. Before we do that, I just want to talk a minute more generally about procedures that existed in 1992. Prior to receiving a request to initiate an investigation from the basic prosecutor what was the role of the investigative judge in the investigation of a crime?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge would move to start an investigation by issuing a decision, and this decision could only be issued if there is a prior request from the prosecution to conduct an investigation. In other words, the investigating judge would conduct the investigation from the moment when the decision is issued and that could only be issued at the request of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, up until the receipt of a request from the prosecutor, the investigative judge did not have any role to play in the investigation up to that point?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat your answer. It didn't come across on the transcript. Up until the point of receiving a request from the prosecutor's office, did the investigative judge play any role in the investigation of the crime at issue?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge did not have any role in this particular case, but also, in general, under the law that was then in force, which was identical to the one before the war, the investigating judge did not have any role and did not conduct any investigation before there was a request issued by the prosecutor to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who was responsible for initiating the criminal justice process? How was the process started?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question? What do you mean by how would the proceedings start? Do you mean the investigating proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is before -- before the investigative judge becomes even involved in the case. How did the process begin? How did a crime become known and enter into the entire criminal justice process, including the prosecutor and then, eventually, the court.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this -- this was a preliminary proceedings. In fact, the criminal proceedings began from the moment when the investigating judge issues a decision to conduct an investigation. Everything prior to that was considered preliminary proceedings. In other words, the discovery of the crime of the perpetrators and in -- at the stage where there was a suspicion, a grounded suspicion that a crime had been committed, then it would have been the prosecutor, in co-operation with the police who would be responsible for that phase. When I say "a suspicion," that would be -- the basis for suspicion that would be the lower degree of suspicion, which was not sufficient to initiate proceedings, and only when the investigating judge actually issues a decision to conduct a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise. We missed the very last portion of your answer. Could you just repeat that.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: When the investigating judge issues a decision to conduct an investigation, that decision is issued on the basis of the prior request to conduct an investigation from the prosecutor, and the prosecutor would have to have collected, together with the police, information and possible evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Whose responsibility was it to identify and arrest the perpetrator of a crime?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by who was responsible or whose responsibility was it? Maybe something was lost in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's right. Whose responsibility was it to identify a perpetrator and arrest that perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The discovery and prosecution of perpetrators was within the competence of the prosecutor. But all of that would relate to the stage where evidence is collected and information. But the initiating of the criminal proceedings on the basis of -- when there is cause to suspect that a crime had been committed, that was done by the investigating judge. So the investigating judge was the individual who actually initiated or officially started the proceedings when there were -- there was a cause to suspect that a crime had been committed and it was sufficient grounds to initiate criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to focus on these preliminary proceedings, not when it comes to the investigative judge. In the preliminary stages, so when the crime is first discovered, who had the responsibility to identify and arrest the perpetrator of a crime? Was it the police; was it the prosecutor? Who actually went out and identified the perpetrator and arrested him?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Under the Law on Criminal Proceedings that was in force at the time there were various organs that were in charge of identifying and discovering perpetrators of criminal offences. There were different types of criminal offences, and one of those roles was on the organs of the interior. Once information was collected and it was learned that a crime had been committed, the police began collecting information and evidence, always in co-operation with the prosecution on the crime. But the prosecutor at the time could not collect any evidence on his own, nor could he or she conduct an investigation, nor would any information that he would obtain at such a stage have any legal force because, at the time, under that law, neither the police nor the prosecutor could investigate or question witnesses or suspects during the preliminary stage. They would only interview or, rather, prepare statements of -- from the suspects, and they had no other role. And that is the reason why the investigating judge would then proceed to question the witnesses and collect evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And please make sure you speak a little bit slower. I think the interpreter is having a little bit of trouble keeping up with you. But as I understand your answer, is that the police, at the preliminary stages, would interview suspects, interview witnesses, collect evidence, but it was the investigative judge's role later on to actually take records of interviews and review that evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about -- that's about right. So the police did not have the jurisdiction to compile records of interviews with the suspects, nor witness interviews. They collected and -- they collected and compiled statements that could not be used as evidence later during the trial itself. So the criminal proceedings begin at the moment when a decision is issued to conduct an investigation, and under the Law on Criminal Proceedings, that was -- that referred to the moment when a criminal report is submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Until a perpetrator is identified, could the investigative judge conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. The investigating judge could only conduct an investigation into a -- perpetrators who are identified, who have been identified, never against perpetrators who have not been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I wanted to briefly talk about on-site investigations. What was the role of the investigative judge in an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: An on-site investigation is one of the phases of the investigation. If it was necessary to conduct an on-site investigation, the organs of the interior would call the investigating judge, and if the investigating judge was present during the on-site investigation, then the judge would actually be in charge of the on-site investigation. Then there would be a report on the on-site investigation, compiled by the investigating judge, if he or she was present. And then this would be used as a basis that could later be used as evidence in the -- in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who did the investigative judge submit the on-site investigation report to?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge would draft notes about the on-site investigation, including the measures that needed to be taken after the on-site investigation. And those notes, or that record, was then forwarded to the prosecutor's office and to the organs of the interior. That is to say, to those who were involved in the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what were the police -- the organs of the interior supposed to do with the report, once they receive it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: If there was evidence found, such as objects, and if a record was made, or if an expert opinion was sought, then that was under the competence of the police in keeping with the record of the on-site investigation. Such objects, for example, such evidence, would be deposited with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, in addition to that, would they collect other information about the crime? Would they look for suspects? Would they interview individuals with regard to the potential crime?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 of the document that we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see -- we can see that -- that the accused in this criminal report or this request are suspected of setting up a check-point in Zvornik at which they appropriated passenger vehicles and other items. Ms. Simeunovic, as an investigative judge, could you go beyond the criminal report and the request for the investigation and investigate crimes that were outside the scope of those documents?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Under the Law on Criminal Proceedings, an investigating judge could not go beyond any such documents, in the sense that it could not include a different type of crime or other perpetrators. Based on this request, the entire case would be viewed in that regard and appropriate indication was sought. If the investigating judge would realise in the course of the proceedings that there are other types of crime involved, he was duty-bound to notify the public prosecutor. In this particular case, the prosecutor was present throughout and was accordingly notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the prosecutor supposed to do with this information about additional crimes?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: He should issue a request, asking for an amendment to the original request for investigation so as to include other crimes and perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And would the prosecutor also contact the police to initiate some initial preliminary investigations into that allegation?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would. Everything had to be tied in with the investigation that is ongoing. As of the moment the decision is issued, the investigative judge could issue orders to the police. If they found other evidence about other crimes and perpetrators, then that fell under the authority of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Olmsted. One intervention in the transcript, page 45, 14, I believe the witness said the investigative judge could issue orders to the police. And it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, could we clarify that. Who would ask the police to take investigative measures if there was a discovery of a new crime during the course of an investigation? Was it the investigative judge or would it be the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: If the investigating judge, based on the documents and evidence attached, including statements, realised that the case involved other perpetrators and crimes, he would notify the prosecutor. Anything that had to do with the investigation itself initiated by the investigating judge by his original request, in terms of any investigative measures, he could turn to the police and ask them to undertake certain investigative measures that the investigating judge was unable to do himself or herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And would those be in the form of a request; or would you be ordering the police that they must carry out those tasks?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was precisely put in the question, in the sense of whether it would be a request or an order. One could pick up the phone and call the police, telling them what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But if I understand you correctly, did the investigative judge exercise supervisor authority over the police? Could the investigative judge punish the police if they didn't carry out an instruction?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how would that come about? Would they file an action against the police; or would they report the police officer to his superior officer?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Such things happen seldom. However, in such a case, a letter would be sent to the chief of police, I believe, or someone higher up in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
