utterances.text: And if we could look under item number 4, we see that the prosecutor is requesting pre-trial detention under Article 191, paragraph 2, item 3, of the Criminal Procedure Code. Was this a mandatory detention?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was not mandatory detention. If there were reasons to believe that -- if there were reasons to issue a detention order, then it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When was pre-trial detention mandatory, in what cases?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to put it this way: Given that that law has not been in use for seven years now, the Law on Criminal Proceedings which was in place before the war and up until 2003, it's difficult for me to tell you anything with any degree of certainty, without referring back to the law itself and its articles. Hence, I would put a hedge here. I believe all attorneys, judges, and everyone one involved always have a copy of that law with us. If would have been far easier for me if I had been given a copy so that I could refer to the particular article. However, as far as I recall, I remember a provision in Article 191, when there was a mention -- where there was a mention of mandatory detention, in case of such crimes which could receive sentences of over ten years or even death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. We have the Criminal Procedure Code and we can look at it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01532, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can have on the screen, P322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, while that is being loaded, I should alert counsel that the -- I have been advised the that the simple course would be break at the usual time. So we would be taking the break at 5.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Simeunovic, we're looking at the criminal charges against Vuckovic et al dated 8 August 1992. Can you confirm whether this is the criminal report that you received along with your request to initiate an investigation.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive it alongside my request, or the prosecutor's request. But, in any case, this was the criminal report which accompanied the request for investigation submitted by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6 of the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we can see at the bottom of the B/C/S version that the report included a number of enclosures, including signed statements made by the perpetrators, the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can now have the screen, 65 ter 3020.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a statement by Vojin Vuckovic dated 6 August 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask Mr. Olmsted, when calling up documents, he could tell us the tab number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is tab 23, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is this a signed statement by one of the perpetrators in this case that you would have received along with a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this statement, you can see that the record was made by -- well, it says in the first paragraph that it's actually a record about an interview with Zuco. There is the type of statement the police took, not in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure, but in their own police way during the pre-trial phase. By virtue of Article 151, as we could see a moment ago in the criminal report, as of the moment ... in the Law on Criminal Procedure we could see what the police are supposed to do as of the moment a criminal report is submitted. That's in Article 151. Before that moment in time, the police -- or, rather, organs of the interior as it was called then, submitted such records as this one, as statements. This statement was one of the attachments to the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 5 of the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see on this page that Vuckovic discusses an incident regarding vehicles seized at the check-point which resulted in an intervention of SJB Pale chief, Malko Koroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn now to page 7 of the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can also see that Vuckovic describes an incident involving Momcilo Mandic actually at the check-point. Do you recall receiving this information?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was following the page on the screen, but this did not tally with what you said because it -- it is found on a different page. In any case, everything contained in this statement is what was uttered by the suspect and, later on, the accused, after an appropriate decision was issued. He did say in this statement given to the police that he been to Pale where he met with this person - what was the name - Koroman, as well as with Biljana Plavsic and Velibor Ostojic. I can't recall what the topic of their discussion was though. In any case, I think it had to do with some vehicles being provided for him to be used. I don't know what follows because I don't know what is on page 5. I still do not see it. On the other pages, he speaks about how they stopped different people, appropriated some vehicles which were then taken to certain locations, or their own houses or houses of people they trusted. He also mentioned who the people at the check-point were ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01533, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps, Your Honours, this would be a good time to recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still haven't seen page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, actually, you answered my question, and so I didn't want to go into any more discussion about this particular statement. And we're taking a break. But if you want to look at it after the break, that's -- I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we start with --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one small intervention before Mr. Olmsted resumes. I apologise for having failed to react on time, although I still am not overdue, I believe. I see a number of statements among the Prosecutor's documents including those who were suspected of having committed certain crimes and who belonged to the Yellow Wasps groups. Those statements were given to the Bijeljina police station, for example, of Vojin Vuckovic's statement, aka Zuco, the Prosecutor sought to tendered that document. It is tab 23, 65 ter 3020. My intervention is as follows: I believe we ought to make it clear with Mr. Olmsted what the goal of tendering these statements is. Namely, the people whose statements were taken by the police in that stage of the procedure gave the so-called information statement under the then-regulations and, as such, they did not need to have counsel at that stage. However, as suspects, they could exercise their right to tell the truth or remain silent, or simply not tell the truth. It is precisely because of that, as the witness explained, such statements were not regarded as evidence that could be used in trial during criminal proceedings. Therefore, if the aim of the Prosecutor is to introduce the contents of the statements in -- into the record or into the body of evidence, I object. We cannot do that without hearing the person in question in person. We would then be able to cross-examine him about the contents of his statement. However, if the aim of the Prosecutor is merely to explain the procedure of the pre-trial stage of the procedure, as to the format of statements taken by the police, I do not object against him making a few examples of that. But, in that case, he should limit his questions to the procedure and steer clear of any contents of such statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I -- well, could I hear what you have -- I would have -- I was under the impression that we were dealing with these as -- as -- as examples of the procedure. But are you going further, as Mr. Cvijetic apprehends?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. This does go to procedure but also the contents are admissible as well. My learned friend's arguments really go to the weight of the evidence, whether the person interviewed was advised of their rights or had counsel present, not to its admissibility and this does -- the statement does go to issues that are relevant to this case. I would note that a number of statements similar to this have been already admitted into evidence in this case on that basis as well, both procedurally, as well as for the value of their content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But leaving aside Mr. Cvijetic's point about the procedure about having to be in informed of their rights and whatnot, which, to my mind, is not relevant, I -- although I have just heard you say that a number of these similar statements have been admitted, even though I thought that we were dealing with the fact that these complaints came into the -- were before the -- by the process before the investigative judge, it seems to be a leap to merely put -- establish the fact of these statements and then, as Mr. Cvijetic seems to be objecting to invite the Chamber to -- find -- find the truth of -- of what those charges, for want of a better word were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. This witness has testified that she received this information. She confirmed two particular pieces of information that I think is relevant to this case. And the statements are -- to earlier, some of those came in through a member of this unit at issue who testified before this Tribunal. So those -- this was just another one along with the other ones that have been admitted. As to, you know, the pre-trial procedures, as far as they're granted to a suspect, that's another issue completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But at some point, as you say, there may be a question of what weight is to be attached to this. And there's certainly room for arguments at the end of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. I just wanted to alert the Defence that, yes, we do intend to use it for its content along with other evidence that we have presented at this trial, just like any other piece of evidence we have presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You still have a problem, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, we do, Your Honour. Mr. Olmsted closed off by saying something that I objected to in the first place. He's moving in the direction in which we believe there are reasons to object. He is busy with the contents of those statements and it is our assertion that such statements could not make their way into the evidence of this case, because they were not admissible even under the then-regulation in our country due to all the reasons I mentioned. We cannot introduce the contents of Mr. Vuckovic's statements through an investigative judge. We cannot do that without him being personally in the courtroom. This witness could only testify to the circumstances of such a procedure. We have no problem with that. But if we are using this investigating judge to introduce the contents of, say, ten or 15 statements, then it is inadmissible as evidence before this Chamber, and they were not admissible back then either, precisely because of the reason I mentioned and that is that a suspect is entitled to lie. As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, it seems to me, at this stage it isn't necessary to overcomplicate this matter. Let's proceed. And as I said, it may be a matter of arguments and submissions at the end of the exercise. But I think I understand Mr. Olmsted's point and perhaps the language that I have been using about separating the fact from the truth is -- is misleading in this context. But I think understand what Mr. Olmsted is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to complete the discussion on this matter, I refer Defence counsel to Rule 89(A) of the Rules of Evidence which specifically states that a Chamber shall apply rules of evidence set forth in this section and shall not be bound by the national rules of evidence. I stood up earlier to mention that Ms. Korner would like to address the Trial Chamber for about ten minutes at the end with regard to the Rule 92 bis witnesses, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So whoever is on his feet at 6.45, we have learned from experience that when counsel say 10 minutes, they don't mean 10 minutes by the clock. So we say 15 minutes. So whoever is on his feet at 6.45 would -- would suspend cross-examination, if we would be at that stage, to allow Ms. Korner to deal with her matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have on the screen 65 ter 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I really don't want to disrupt anymore. But Mr. Olmsted was referring to Rule 89(A), and I believe Mr. Olmsted is very well acquainted with the Rule 95, as well. Therefore, the argument on 98 [sic](A) doesn't really stand, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move back to the evidence and we can save this for a later day argument. 65 ter 2488, please. That's tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a decision to conduct investigation dated 25 August 1992. If we could just turn to the last page? Ms. Simeunovic, could you confirm, do you recall issuing this discussion?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01534. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to show you now a few records of interviews. The first one, 65 ter 2385.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is tab 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a record of interview with Dobrivoje Ikonic. And if we could just turn to the last page of the B/C/S. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at 65 ter 2386, which is tab 31. This is a record of interview of Vojin Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see -- is that your signature at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, can we look at 2489. That's tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a record of interview with Nenad Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last page of that; B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These are all records of interviews dated 25 August 1992. Do you recognise these as some of the interviews that you conducted in August?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are interviews that I compiled, or drafted or, rather, statements that the accused were -- during the interview of the accused, as mentioned, Simic Nenad, Vojin Vuckovic, Ikonic, and I don't know what others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who brought the suspects to the interview?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: In every procedure, it envisaged that the police would bring the suspects who were in detention, in police detention. In other words, they were all -- they had already been arrested by the police and kept in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall where they were detained?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Ministry of Justice prisons in operation in Bijeljina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was no prison. So that these persons, I assume, were detained on the premises of the police station, envisaged for detention of individuals that the police arrested up to three days, according to the then-legal prescription, or longer, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to just briefly mention another detention facility, the Bakovic detention facility. To your knowledge, did the court in Bijeljina ever issue any remand orders or conduct any criminal investigations with regard to prisoners held at that facility, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May these three documents be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01535, P01536 and P01537 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have up on the screen P317-21; this is tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again, Your Honours. Just for the clarity of the transcript and that we know where we are, can the -- the, please, the Registrar give us the 65 ter number for each and every of the three exhibits, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 02385 is admitted as Exhibit P01535; 65 ter 02386 is admitted as Exhibit P01536; while 65 ter 02489 is admitted as P01537. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If we may have P317-21 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a ruling suspending detention of Vojin Vuckovic et al dated 28 August 1992. Do you recall issuing this decision?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2 of the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that the reason provided for their release was that the prosecutor had not requested an extension of detention. And from this, you concluded that the prosecutor does not feel there is sufficient reason for detention. Did you consult with the prosecutor before issuing this decision?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I both consulted with the prosecutor and I also submitted, on time, the decision, which is why the time is noted of the issuance of this. And if the prosecutor felt that there were still reasons to detain these person, then they could still -- the prosecutor could still take measures, or act -- asked for measures, but I myself consider that there were no such compelling reasons or grounds to keep them in detention and that is why I issued this ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You reference Article 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Under that Article who could recommend the extension of pre-trial custody?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, I have to say that I cannot say off the top of my head what is -- what is all in Article 197, but the extension of pre-trial custody could only be decided upon by the investigating judge and the prosecutor. If you're referring to Article 197.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I don't believe that the witness said "decided upon." I believe "proposed by." But can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, it's the investigating judge or the prosecutor who proposes to extend the pre-trial detention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that you didn't feel it was necessary to extend their detention. Why not?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Because there was no cause -- or there were no grounds to extend their custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would it have made a difference to you if they were under investigation for a crime punishable by death? In that instance, would you have sought to extend their detention?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, detention would be mandatory, as we already said. And then it would have to be extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2388. That's tab 33, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a request to broaden investigation to include Dusko Vuckovic and is dated the 14th of September, 1992. Do you recall receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And does this document relate to the case against Vojin Vuckovic and others?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: As we said earlier, but we did not really pay any attention to that, in the criminal complaint that was submitted by the police or perhaps the public security station in Bijeljina, it was stated that this individual, too, had committed, among other, this criminal offence, but that this individual was handed over to the military court or prosecutor, I'm not sure but we can see it in that criminal report, and that two individual who are also mentioned in the criminal report were at large. And as for Vuckovic, for Dusko Vuckovic, it was said that he had been surrendered to the military court, or, rather, to the military prosecutor who decided to keep him -- or who issued decision to keep him in custody. And it says so here, that according to the ruling of military court that that was the case but that the military prosecutor has established that they did not have jurisdiction over this individual so they returned the case -- I don't know exactly how the whole thing went because the reasons provided by the prosecutor from Bijeljina does not specify which documents were sent back to the police or which documents had been submitted by the police. The only thing that is mentioned is at that this was -- this related to the criminal offence of aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let's turn to page 2 of the B/C/S and the English. And along the lines of what you were just stating, it states that the military prosecutor sent the criminal report against Dusko Vuckovic back to the civilian prosecutor with the explanation that this accused could not be treated as a member of the Serbian army, because, just as the other individuals referenced in the criminal report, he was not a member of the regular armed forces. Under the law at the time, which courts had jurisdiction over crimes committed by paramilitary groups against civilians?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: What criminal offences are you referring to? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, here it is just giving a justification for sending it back to the civilian prosecutors that this person was not a member of the regular armed forces. And so I'm just talking generally if a member of a paramilitary group commits a crime, let's say against a civilian, would that be within the jurisdiction of the civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, that would depend on the type of criminal offence. At that time, and I don't know, again I have to say, what it was that the police submitted to the military prosecutor. I can only assume that he was either a military -- he was either a soldier or had committed a criminal offence that would fall under criminal offences -- under war crimes or a similar crime. So this is what we see also here in the reasons why it was sent to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you answered my question. They sent this case back to the civilian prosecutor and this person was found not to be a member of the regular Serbian army. So my question to you is, that was a basis under the law to send a case to the civilian prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: If he committed the criminal offence of theft as appears from this request to expand the investigation, in that case, the jurisdiction would be with the lower prosecutor's office. However, if the criminal offence had to do with war crimes, those cases were then under the jurisdiction of the military court and the military prosecutor. And from this request we don't see any of that. We don't see that I was sent any accompanying documents, as the investigating judge, and there's just an explanation that this was returned because this person was not a member of the armed forces and no other criminal offences are mentioned, other than the criminal offence of theft. And already at this time he had been released from detention. And from this document, we can see that for a while he was detained pursuant to a decision by the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. You mentioned war crimes. If a civilian person commits a war crime, which court had jurisdiction over that civilian who committed a war crime, if it's not a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in practice, we did not have such cases where a civilian would commit a war crime because I think, in fact, in real life it is not really possible for a civilian to commit a war crime. That person would have to be either a member of the armed forces or a member of paramilitary units. But at this time, and I can't really tell you right now why, whether there was a Law on Military Courts which provided for this, but I know that criminal offences, regardless of perpetrator, would be submitted to the military prosecutor and the military court, if they involved war crimes. So they were not treated -- they were not within the jurisdiction of the lower court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you would agree we would have to look at the Law on Military Courts to determine that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say again that, after all this time, I can't really ascertain that, nor do have I that Law on Military Court before me. But as far as I remember, and as far as I know, all the cases involving war crimes were prosecuted by military prosecutors and military courts. Why and how, I really don't know, and I don't think that I'm an expert on the issue and that I could really say anything with certainty why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you grant this request to broaden the investigation?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I assumed that I did. There was no reason not to, I think, because we can't see here that there is any mention of any war crimes or anything else because this individual was already included in the original criminal report for theft. And just as there was a request to conduct an investigation for the other individuals, this was just an expansion of that same request to conduct an investigation into this individual, based on that original criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 1D00-5204; that's a document ID number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we have a tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Tab number 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a statement by Dusko Vuckovic taken by the military police in Bijeljina dated 4 August 1992. Did you receive this statement back in 1992 when the case against Dusko Vuckovic was transferred to the civilian court?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never received this statement. And if it says in the heading that this was prosecuted by the military police, then they would have interviewed this suspect, according to the instruction from the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In this statement, Vuckovic admits to a number of crimes against Muslim detainees at the Celopek cultural centre in Zvornik. During the course of your investigation, did you ever receive informing regarding these crimes committed by either Dusko Vuckovic or other members of the Yellow Wasps against non-Serbs from either the civilian police, or the military police, or any other source?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I could not really determine with certainty the time when this occurred, but I know that there was a call from one of the courts in Sabac, which is in Serbia, and that they did not tell me all the details but they said that their -- they had initiated proceedings against this individual. I can't recall the details. Because -- or for criminal offences committed in Zvornik and they asked me to submit all the files that I had and documents that I had at my disposal and I suppose that I sent the entire court file. I can't recall the details, but I do know that I was in contact with the Sabac court because they were the ones conducting the proceedings for war crimes against this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that was a civilian court, the one in Sabac?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I assume that that was the case. You can probably ascertain that from documents. I'm sure you have documents to show which type of court it -- it was, whether it was the lower court, the district court or senior court or maybe a military court, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now back in August 1992, if you had received this statement or any information from the civilian or military police about these crimes at the Celopek cultural centre what would you have done, what actions would have you taken with regard to your criminal investigation in this matter?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for one, if I did receive -- if I had received this, and I didn't, and now we're just hypothesising here, so seeing that this was handled by the military police and knowing that this individual was detained probably pursuant to a ruling by the military court, I would first get in touch with the prosecutor, or, rather, with the president of my court, we would then discuss it in the collegium, and I'm certain that we would have taken some steps, and this person would not have been released from custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not on our exhibit list, but it was provided to us by the Defence, amongst other documents. I would move at this time for it to be added to our 65 ter list and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection from us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Defence, not objecting, the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01539. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen P317-19; this is tab 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, while you're winding down to the 6.45 mark for Ms. Korner's matter, I would alert you that at that point you would have exhausted the extended time that you requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have before us is the indictment against Vuckovic et al dated 13 September 1999 and includes both Dusko Vuckovic and Vojin Vuckovic. By the time of the filing of this indictment you had left the basic court, but can you tell us between 1992 and 1996, is it correct that this case remained in the investigative phase of the criminal justice system?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At any point during that period, did the investigation expand beyond crimes of the thefts at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not, except for what I said earlier, that I had information that proceedings were initiated against Vuckovic, Dusko for war crimes. How these proceedings were initiated, whether it was trigged -- whether he -- Dusko Vuckovic was transferred from the -- from a military prison in Bijeljina to Sabac or in some other way, I don't know. I can't say anything about this case because I was not involved with anything to do with this case, up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand, and we don't want you to talk about something that you weren't participating in. But with regard to this case before the Bijeljina Basic Court, were the charges expanded beyond the crimes at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I cannot speak about things that I have no information about. I was not aware of this indictment either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did this case against the members of the Yellow Wasps ever result in a trial?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really have no knowledge. I mean, that would not be difficult to find out. You could check if you inquired with the court in question. Based on this indictment, could you see what transpired and what phase of the proceedings that case is in, whether it has already been -- whether a sentence has already been, and a judgement issued, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 1535. It's tab 58. And this is the Bijeljina basic prosecutor's office KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During proofing on Sunday, you had a chance to review the entries in this KT log-book from the period 1 April to 31 December 1992. Can you tell us how many murder or voluntary manslaughter cases you were able to identify in which the victim was a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did look at this log-book, and I informed myself about the crimes committed. In that period of time, there was a number of murders, although I do not recall the number anymore. There was only one murder in which the victim or the person who was killed was a Muslim. There were far more murders with Serbian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at page 32 of the B/C/S; page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can zoom in on entry 223, we see a criminal report by SJB Bijeljina received on 5 August 1992 for an Article 36 crime with a victim of the name Salko Kukic. Was this the non-Serb murder case that you were able to identify in this log-book?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since we have limited time, let's look at one more entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 35 of the B/C/S; page 9 of the English. I'm sorry, actually page 40 of the B/C/S; page 10 of the English. And if we could zoom in on entry 244.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what we see under entry 244 is a criminal report by SJB Bijeljina against Vojin Vuckovic and others for aggravated theft. Is this the Yellow Wasps case that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that was the case. I don't know whether I saw it in any other log-books, but I do know that there was another murder in 1992, although I don't remember any longer in which of the log-books I saw it, if I did. I do know there was a murder of three Muslims at the time. It was an elderly couple and another younger person, and I don't remember anymore whether I saw it in any log-book or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01540. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very quickly, if we can have 65 ter 2757 on the screen; this is tab 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a decision to discontinue investigation in the case against Slaven Lukic et al dated 24 August 1992. We just looked at the KT entry for the case involving the murder of -- of Salko Kukic. If we look at the last two paragraphs of the B/C/S, page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We need to turn to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that the investigation was discontinued with the explanation that the military prosecutor informed the investigating judge that he decided to abandoned the prosecution of the accused. Ms. Simeunovic, can you tell us, do you know why the prosecution of the Kukic murder case was discontinued, abandoned?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning this case and the proceedings around that, well, that's something I never had anything to do with. What I do know, however, is that after this person was found dead, the victim, Slavko Kukic, the basic court in Bijeljina, or, rather, their investigative judge, and the duty prosecutor, as well as the police, i.e., the Bijeljina station carried out an on-site investigation. The police gathered information and detected the perpetrator. They followed up with a criminal report submitted to the basis prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. Given that the perpetrators were military personnel, as we can see here from the military police, the entire case file was forwarded to the military court in Bijeljina. As for why the prosecutor abandoned any further investigation, that is something I don't know, and it doesn't say here. I do know, however, that the case was officially closed, although I don't know when exactly. I also know that all of the perpetrators received their sentences. I don't know whether they're still in jail, but I do know that a final decision was made in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The trial against them, was that -- was that during the conflict or after it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to show you one more document. It's 65 ter 2966.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, yes, I apologise, tab 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have before us is the Bijeljina basic prosecutor's office KTN or unknown perpetrator log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 4 of the B/C/S; page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We've just a moment ago looked at the KT log-book. Now we have in front of us the KTN log-book. During your proofing, you had a chance to review the 11 entries in this log-book for the period between 1 April and 31 December 1992, all of which appear on the two pages that we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we can turn the B/C/S one so it faces the right direction. And let's zoom in a little bit, at least on the first page, the page on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you reviewed this log-book, were you able to identify any entries for murders or voluntary manslaughter of non-Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. This is so small that I can't read. I can only speak off the cuff about what I can recall about the three victims. I don't really know whether they are in this log-book. At that time, the perpetrators were still unknown. However, in 1993, or in late 1992, the perpetrators were discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: But I can't read this now, and I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But during your -- and I don't want to talk about that particular case that you think you recollect from 1993. But if you could tell us -- you reviewed this log-book during proofing and when you reviewed it in proofing, were you able to identify any murder or manslaughter cases involving non-Serb victims, just from reviewing these pages?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: During proofing, as now, I said that it would be less than serious on my part to comment any log-books of the prosecution which I had never seen before, and there was no need for me to do so as the investigating judge. The writing here is far too small. I did not have sufficient time and simply cannot comment on any of these documents. I had no role to play in their creation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could move to the right-hand page I want to look quickly at the last entry. Entry, I believe, it's 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see that the unknown perpetrator report for this crime is under Article 144 of the SFRY Criminal Code. Would that be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head. I would really need to refer to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The victims listed are Ljubomir and Dragomir Tanic. Could you tell us what their ethnicity would have been?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose Serbs, but not necessarily. There could have been Croats. I don't think there were Bosniaks though, but I'd rather not go into that now. It's really not something I can tell you anything about specifically. As for Article 144, I would have to have the law before me to know what the crime in question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What basis, Mr. Olmsted, having regard to every answer the witness has given.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, to a certain degree, the log-book speaks for itself. We have the SFRY Criminal Code. We can look up what Article 144 is. So this is a relevant document in this case. Now that she is not able to answer my questions entirely, that's -- you know, that's her testimony, but the document itself is relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document may be relevant and may be admissible not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's mark it for exhibit -- identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01542, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Final question, Ms. Simeunovic. To your knowledge, were any criminal reports filed in 1992 against police officers for committing crimes against non-Serbs, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Madam, we're about to take the adjournment for today. Your testimony is not at an end because there's still cross-examination to come. We will resume in this courtroom at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. The Court will not rise at this point because it has some procedural matters with which to deal, so the usher will escort you from the courtroom. But I must caution you to having been sworn as a witness you cannot have any communication whatever with counsel from either side and in such conversations as you may have with anyone outside the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony before the Tribunal. So you will return to this courtroom for 2.15 tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, good afternoon. I'm here because of the matters that were raised yesterday and because I have rather more knowledge of the nuts and boats perhaps of this whole saga, if I can put it that way, than Mr. Hannis. Your Honours, can I return to the question of the 92 bis witnesses as proposed by the Prosecution in their motion. First, Your Honours, yesterday as Mr. Hannis referred to earlier this afternoon, ordered us to provide the timings and we will do so by Thursday. The timings for these witnesses, if they are viva voce, now, if -- we understood Your Honours want to know this for the purposes of scheduling, but if we're wrong, and the purpose is because Your Honours intend that we should call all the witnesses via, well, then what I have to say today will be moot. But we have understood it purely if the Defence don't agree then Your Honours are jumping straight from 92 bis, if the Defence want the witnesses to attend for cross-examination to via, without the intermediate step of 92 ter which is catered for under Rule (C) of 92 bis. Your Honours, going back to July - it seems a long time ago now - we had various discussions in open court with Your Honours about how the Defence were going to notify us and the Court whether they would agree to these witnesses being 92 bis. There was a lengthy discussion on the 15th of July, and Mr. Zecevic then made it clear that the Defence could not or would not be able to say whether they agreed 92 bis witnesses until such time as we had provided all the disclosure, not just the statements or the transcripts, but all the disclosure that comes from doing the full search on a witness. Your Honours, despite the discussion, and, indeed, despite later discussions and the discussion yesterday, the position, as I understand it from the Defence, is quite clear and I just want to make sure that Your Honours understand it. They are not prepared to say, as Mr. Zecevic indicated, whether they will accept the witness testimony under the terms of 92 bis until such time as we do full disclosure. So we're now with the great what I call the -- the great ever decreasing circles theory. We have spent the last few weeks over the adjournment, asking for the full searches to be done on each of these witnesses, in order of how we intended to call them, which meant the viva voce witnesses first. ISU, like everywhere else in this Tribunal, has had reduced staff as we have, and over the summer break. So the searchs are coming in, in batches. We have not yet got a single 92 bis search back. Therefore, in order, as Mr. Zecevic, and I understand also Mr. Krgovic, want full disclosure before they'll agree to this, plus the highlighting on the statements, that will not be done, us filing a 92 bis motion until such time as we can get the searches back. So nothing can be decided by the original estimate, let alone September the 3rd. Because we've got to get all the searches back, then we've got to put the material together, then we've got to do the highlighting, and so there will be a delay. So therefore, Your Honours, I want to make it absolutely plain to Your Honours, that, really, tomorrow's meeting and any discussion between us and the Defence at this stage based only on the statements isn't going to get us anywhere unless Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Zecevic can be persuaded to at least indicate whether or not they accept, subject to searchs coming back, and, at the moment, that I'm told that's not possible. So it seemed to me Your Honours ought to be put in the picture. Either we -- we -- we stop the searches. We highlight. We take what we've got, what we know we've got that applies for the witnesses from the previous testimony in each case of the documents and what I'm given to the Defence or we have to wait, as Mr. Zecevic indicated he wants full disclosure, in which case, nothing is going to be done -- well, nothing will be ready for some time to come. So that's the situation I'm afraid we're in at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Could -- could I just ask for clarification. If disclosure of the statements and the testimonies of the 44 witnesses has been made to the Defence so that what we're talking about is only the additional evidence that might occur as a result of the full search. So the -- the -- the mandatory disclosure, according to the Rules, are the statements and transcripts, has been made for all the witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That was done, in fact, I think I told Your Honour even before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But without highlights.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Without highlights. But if we now -- can I just add to that, as I say it's the ever decreasing circles theory. If we take the staff now to do the highlighting, that's the lawyers because they're the only people who can really deal with it, then we will no longer be reviewing the searches as they come in, because we will have to stop doing that to do the highlighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe our position was very clear. The 92 bis rule requires the Prosecution to provide the documents, highlighted portions of the testimonies or the statements of the -- of the witnesses, which it intends to -- to offer as 92 bis. That is the -- that is the first step. When we reached that first step, we will be probably able to give some indication. But before we receive that, we are not able to give any indication. That is the point. Now, the -- the -- the overall searches, I don't think they have anything to do with this, with the clear obligation of the Prosecution to give us the highlighted portions of the statements and the testimonies of the witnesses which they are intending to call as 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's actually -- sorry, have you finished Mr. Zecevic? It's not actually what Mr. Zecevic said either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. I seem to recall, Mr. Zecevic, that the full search was actually done at your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours, yes. But it doesn't -- Your Honours, we need the full search, the full disclosure on these witnesses. We need that which is only normal obligation of the Prosecution to provide us with the disclosure. Your Honours, for the purposes of cross-examining, I'm not talking about the 92 bis. The 92 bis -- the Rules for the 92 bis, the Prosecution has to give us the highlights portions of the testimonies and statements of the witnesses or the package, the 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the whole point. You see, A, the Rule doesn't require us to highlight. We volunteer that. The Rule says nothing about highlighting. It deals with the qualifications for admission under 92 bis. Nothing about highlighting. We said we would do that, and we will. But what is the -- see we go around ever decreasing circles -- what is the point of us doing the highlighting when the Defence, who must know whether or not they are prepared to accept these witnesses, say, No, we want them to all come viva voce, in which we have wasted how many man hours and time doing the highlighting. As I say, if that's what Your Honours order us to do, and that's what the Defence insist on us doing before they can give any indication, then, Your Honours, we will stop doing any further review of the searches. We will do the highlighting of the statements or the transcripts, and -- and then -- again, will just delay matters further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, am I wrong if I think that independently of the -- the 92 bis question, that your office is making this full search anyhow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. It is obliged to, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, am I wrong in my understanding that you say now that, for the 92 bis business, you don't need the full search?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will try to explain very -- very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me try to [Overlapping speakers] ... say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to answer. Your Honours, we -- the -- I will take one example. We have the -- I have before me the -- the motion filed on the 29th February 2008 in this case in the pre-trial phase, and this is the 92 bis motion filed by the same Prosecution. The motion contains annex, for example, A, and it says in comments, it says name of the -- the person, the witness, the transcript, the date, everything relevant counts of the indictment, and so on. And it says in comments: Portions covered by adjudicated facts are highlighted in blue, other relevant portions are highlighted in yellow. And those are the packages of 92 bis statements which have been admitted into this case and offered to be admitted in this case. So I don't see why the Prosecution doesn't follow the same procedure which they -- designated in this case. It was my understanding when they filed the motion for 54 new witnesses they already knew the portions of the documents for these witnesses who are going to be called as 92 bis witnesses. So I don't see what is the problem. The problem is, for us, before we receive the -- this, we don't know where to look at. That's one thing. And the second thing is, before we receive the full disclosure, we cannot say whether we want this -- this person to come to -- for cross-examination or not. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you saying more than you said ten minutes ago. So now you say you need the full search?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Rule -- the Rule of 92 bis, it is the obligation of the -- of the Prosecution ongoing obligation to provide us with the disclosure and they are doing it. They -- they continually search the documents or the -- or the database for the witnesses and provide us with Rule 68 and 66, and so on, documents. Your Honours what we need now is -- is -- is indication what are we supposed to look at and that is the highlighted portions [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... have a very important indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All these witnesses will only come to testify about adjudicated facts that have been denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I -- I appreciate that. And I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's very important information when you go through all those -- those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honours, one witness comes to testify, for example, for adjudicated fact 467, let's say. The Prosecution knows that this witness talks about the -- the adjudicated fact 467, otherwise, they wouldn't call him. So, in -- in order to facilitate our -- our work, they have to give us a highlighted portion of the testimony which lasted for seven days which is 3.000 pages long. If we are to go through each and every witness for -- for a number of days that they testified, it will take us -- it will take us another six months, Your Honours, to be able to -- and I don't really see why is that a problem for the Prosecution to -- to indicate to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If -- if I may, the issue turns on the marking of the statements and the testimony. So let's address that first. For the 44 witnesses that are now in play, the Prosecution has provided, if I understand it correctly, all the statements and the testimonies for those witnesses. But these statements and testimonies, unfortunately, are -- have not yet been marked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. So one issue would be or one question would be, how soon could the Prosecution identify in those statements and transcripts the portions that are relevant to the denied adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will take considerable time to do that. And it is -- can I just say this. It's a waste of effort if, at the end of the day the Defence know already that they are not -- that they are going to seek to ask for the witnesses to be called viva voce and so just attending for cross-examinations. We can do it, but I say now, we consider it a waste of effort if the Defence are going -- know now that they are going to ask for these people to be cross-examined. And secondly, in order to do it, within a reasonable time-limit, every lawyer will stop doing the review of the searches and disclosure and do just that. But can he with certainly do it. And I would estimate it will take two to three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. Because as far as I have understood, there is a distinction to be made between, on the one hand, the testimonies and the statements that have already been disclosed to the Defence and, on the other hand, possible extra searches in the rest of the Prosecution's documentary base, in which there might pop up, eventually, new indications or information relating to those witnesses, but that are certainly over and above the statements and the testimonies of witnesses. And -- and -- and my understanding, if -- if -- if I have understood this correctly, is that to do this extra search, to look for extra small things that might pop up somewhere is a very laborious effort and that will take immense time. But if we revert and go back to the statements in the transcript that have already been disclosed, my assumption would be that it would not -- it would, of course, be a laborious enterprise. It would not be that difficult and that consuming to have electronic searches made in order to identify the parts of those testimonies and statements that are relevant to the denied adjudicated facts. That, I would assume, could be done in a reasonably shorter time than to complete the full search.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it could. No question about that, Your Honours. When you say shorter time, we're still talking weeks and as His Honour Judge Delvoie pointed out, the Defence know that these witnesses have been picked because they cover the adjudicated facts, and they are able to say, all of these witnesses have obviously, or nearly all, I think, have testified before and the Defence must know whether they are going to -- to want them to attend for cross-examination because it is not accepted. Your Honours, I -- I am also not clear why it is so difficult in the sense that I don't know what the situation is going to be about cross-examination, but if there is a limitation on -- on -- what the witnesses can say in-chief, in other words just giving the context and dealing with the adjudicated fact, then if there's a limitation again on the Defence, we don't know what Your Honours intend to do about that, but they can only cross-examine on those restricted matters. I see Judge Harhoff nodding, well, then they don't need the searches anyhow. So, I mean, the only reason I brought this to Your Honours' attention today is, as I say, because I don't think Your Honours were quite clear on the divide between us. And if Your Honours agree with Mr. Zecevic that we should do the highlighting, then we will do it, but we will, as I say, not be dealing -- for the moment until that exercise is done with anything that arises from searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we have gone long past the time for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. Can I -- I know -- I appreciate -- I know the interpreters have been here since 2.15, but I wonder if Your Honours could feel able to give an indication today, now, if not, because we are not sitting tomorrow -- or perhaps sit tomorrow. Oh so we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are sitting tomorrow in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, we are. I had forgot that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But to summarise, it is more or less a vicious circle. You do the highlighting or they do the highlighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, they don't do it with a pen but they have to make the search that you do by highlighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's one. Second thing is, we're talking about 29 witnesses proposed to be heard as 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We do. Okay. So I would say let's -- let's get back to tomorrow and eventually to the estimates you will give us on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes. Absolutely, Your Honours, yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we apologise to the interpreters and the court reporter for entrenching on their time. We take the adjournment to 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of August, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
